Series::floor_divide¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::floor_divide(const Series& other) const
Series Series::floor_divide(double other) const
Series& Series::floor_divide_(const Series& other)
Series& Series::floor_divide_(double other)
Series& Series::floor_divide_(const Series& rhs) const
Series& Series::floor_divide_(double rhs) const

What It Does¶

Divides elementwise and rounds the quotient toward negative infinity:

floor_divide(a, b) = floor(a / b)

This is true floor division, so the direction is determined by the number line, not by the sign of the operands. floor_divide(-7, 2) is -4, not -3, while floor_divide(-8, -3) is 2 because the quotient is positive.

It pairs with remainder(). For every nonzero divisor, the two operations preserve the Euclidean reconstruction:

a = floor_divide(a, b) * b + remainder(a, b)

The remainder follows the divisor’s sign. Choosing floor_divide() rather than truncating division is therefore not only a rounding decision; it determines which remainder convention makes the reconstruction hold.

Dtype follows type promotion of the inputs: two integral operands give an integral result; anything floating gives a floating result. For the scalar overload, an integer-valued scalar against an integral series keeps the result integral; a fractional scalar makes it floating.

Parameters¶

other (const Series& or double): the divisor b. A Series broadcasts against the receiver; a double applies the same divisor everywhere.

Returns¶

Series or Series& floor(a / b), integral when both operands are integral, otherwise floating. floor_divide_() writes the result back into the receiver.

Gradient¶

floor_divide() is a rounding operation with a locally constant value, so it is not differentiable — a reverse pass through it alone raises. For a differentiable quotient use div().

In-Place Form¶

floor_divide_() is the in-place sibling of floor_divide(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — floor_divide_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({7.0, -7.0, 8.0}, {3});
auto y = pluss::make_series({2.0, 2.0, 2.0}, {3});

x.floor_divide_(y);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[3, -4, 4]

auto x = pluss::make_series({7.0, -7.0, 8.0}, {3});
x.floor_divide_(2.0);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[3, -4, 4]

Examples¶

Example 1. All four sign combinations make the rounding direction visible.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({7, -7, 8, -8})
        .floor_divide(pluss::make_series({2, 2, -3, -3})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[3, -4, -3, 2]

-7 / 2 = -3.5 floors to -4. Likewise, 8 / -3 is approximately -2.67 and floors to -3; changing both signs makes -8 / -3 positive, so it floors to 2.

Example 2. Floating operands give a floating result.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({7.5, -7.5}).floor_divide(pluss::make_series({2.0, 2.0})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[3.0000, -4.0000]

Example 3. A fractional scalar promotes an integral receiver to floating point.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({7, 8}).floor_divide(2.5));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[2.0000, 3.0000]

The receiver is int64, but 2.5 cannot be represented as an integer divisor, so the operation promotes before dividing. By contrast, floor_divide(2.0) recognizes the scalar as integer-valued and keeps an integral result.

Example 4. The in-place form is appropriate only when the result fits the receiver’s existing shape and dtype.

auto values = pluss::make_series({7, -7});
const void* storage = values.raw_data();

values.floor_divide_(2.0);
pluss::series::print(std::cout, values) << '\n';
std::cout << "same storage: " << std::boolalpha
          << (storage == values.raw_data());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[3, -4]
same storage: true

An integer-valued scalar leaves the result in int64, so this update is safe. Replacing 2.0 with 2.5 would require a floating result and therefore cannot be performed in place on this integer receiver; use floor_divide(2.5) instead.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • It floors, it does not truncate: a negative quotient rounds away from zero. For truncation toward zero, use div() then trunc().

  • Two integer operands give an integer result; do not expect a float back from int.floor_divide(int).

  • A zero divisor has no valid integer floor quotient. Validate or mask divisors before calling when zero is possible; do not build an algorithm around a backend-specific inf or NaN result from floating division by zero.

  • floor_divide_() preserves storage. It rejects a broadcast that changes the receiver shape and a result dtype that cannot be stored safely in the receiver.

  • Not differentiable.

Summary¶

floor_divide(a, b) is floor(a / b):

  • rounds toward negative infinity, including for negative results

  • integral in, integral out; floating otherwise (scalar: integral only for an integer-valued scalar)

  • pairs with remainder()

  • not differentiable; floor_divide_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::remainder: the matching divisor-signed modulo.

  • Series::div: the un-rounded, differentiable quotient.

  • Series::fmod: the truncated-division remainder (pairs with truncation toward zero, not flooring).
